paper.title: SkillClaw: Let Skills Evolve Collectively with Agentic Evolver
paper.central_claim: SkillClaw turns trajectories from many users into shared evidence, uses an autonomous agentic evolver to refine or create skills in a shared repository, validates candidates nightly against the deployed best skill pool and synchronizes accepted skills to all agents, so that skills evolve collectively and significantly improve Qwen3-Max on WildClawBench in real-world agent scenarios.
paper.claim_scope: WildClawBench (60 tasks, 6 domains) with four categories reported, 8 simulated concurrent users, 6 day-night rounds, Qwen3-Max as executor/evolver/validator.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref unavailable to the worker subagent at write time; model_type recorded per controller dispatch instruction (agent_model=haiku slot -> claude-sonnet-5-5[1m]).

signatures.object: Shared skill repository (SKILL.md files: skill body, description, category), non-weight artifact deployed to all agents.
signatures.information: Per-session structured trajectories (prompt, actions, tool feedback, final response; fields truncated ~400 chars), LLM-written 8-15 sentence summary, PRM/ORM scores, tool-error flags, referenced-skill list; full old skill text and (in no-fresh mode) all prior versions and evidence files.
signatures.operation: Group sessions by referenced skill (and a no-skill group); Qwen3-Max agentic evolver chooses improve_skill / optimize_description / create_skill / skip with conservative targeted edits; saves v<N> snapshot and v<N>_evidence before editing.
signatures.output: Candidate skill update; nightly A/B execution of old vs candidate in idle user environments on tasks from the day interaction data; model compares outcomes; Accept if better performance/stability else Reject.
signatures.conditions: Only skills triggered during the day with potential for improvement are candidates; success sessions define invariants; hard constraints on API contracts, ports, paths; prefer skip when in doubt.
signatures.feedback: ORM/PRM scores, tool errors, user feedback inside sessions; validator outcome comparison.
signatures.selection_rule: Candidate must outperform the currently deployed best skill on validation tasks; same-pool retests with higher readings are also marked Accept as new best-so-far.
signatures.selection_data: Tasks selected from the same day interaction data (WildClawBench tasks); no separate held-out set.
signatures.persistence: Accepted skills merged into the shared repository, synchronized to all agents for the next day; rejected candidates kept as records; version history files persist only in --no-fresh mode.
signatures.later_use: Agents see a catalogue of skills in the prompt and load relevant ones for later tasks.
signatures.claimed_effect: Day1->Day6: Social 54.01->60.34, Search 22.73->34.55, Creative 11.57->21.80, Safety 24.00->32.00 (percent score).
signatures.failure_boundary: Many candidates rejected (e.g. every Creative Synthesis candidate after Night 1); same-pool retests move scores without skill change; gains concentrated in one or two accepted skills per category.

signatures.object: Aggregation scope: sessions pooled across users and over time to drive one shared skill set (cross-user knowledge transfer).
signatures.information: Sessions from 8 simulated users, grouped per referenced skill so that the skill is the controlled factor.
signatures.operation: Aggregate then evolve; cross-user claim rests on the argument that diverse contexts reveal the behavioral boundary of a skill.
signatures.output: One shared repository synchronized to everyone.
signatures.later_use: All agents read the same pool.
signatures.failure_boundary: No single-user or no-aggregation control, so the collective effect is not isolated; multi-user is simulated on one benchmark.

gap.author_gap: Skills deployed in agent ecosystems stay static; improvements found in one session or by one user are not consolidated or shared, so every user rediscovers the same fixes; memory methods stay instance-bound and skill methods treat libraries as static.
gap.checked_gap: A real practical limitation (static, per-user skills) is argued, and the cross-user aggregation angle is concrete. However, the claim that skill libraries do not evolve is weakened by the paper own related work, which cites lifelong skill self-evolution, evolving memory skills, and skill refinement works; none is compared experimentally. The unique residue is cross-user aggregation, which is not isolated in experiments.
gap.lineage: Reflection/memory (Reflexion, ExpeL-like) -> skill libraries (Voyager-style, SOP skills) -> single-agent skill evolution -> group-level shared-skill evolution with nightly gated deployment.
closest_adjacent: Single-agent skill evolution and lifelong skill self-evolution cited in Sec.4.2
Memory-based experience reuse (Reflexion etc.) cited in Sec.1
gap.residue: Overlapping task spaces across users produce complementary evidence about a skill behavioral boundary that single-user data cannot supply.
gap.stakes: Repeated rediscovery of the same procedural fixes across users and sessions.
gap.method_response: Centralized evidence aggregation + agentic evolver + nightly A/B validation + synchronization.
gap.remaining_gap: Collective vs single-user effect not tested; no comparison with other skill-evolution baselines; gains measured on the validation task pool; four of six categories reported; small scale.
unresolved: Whether cross-user aggregation (versus per-user evolution) drives any gain.
Whether improvements hold on tasks not used for validation.

rs_pattern.reason: The executed operation is closed-loop maintenance of a shared external artifact: aggregate execution traces across users, edit skill documents, A/B-validate against the incumbent and deploy. None of the 15 original cards defines this operation. adapt_via_conditioning/C03 covers injecting retrieved artifacts into a frozen model but not writing, validating and retaining them; heterogeneous_decomposition would only describe the grouping-by-skill index, which is not the load-bearing treatment.

matches.reason: Pooled multi-user sessions are mined into structured, versioned SKILL.md packages that are merged and quality-filtered (A/B validated) before publication to a shared library, matching the H02 tactic.
Skill defects are separated from agent/environment problems, edits are bounded and conservative, and the revised skill is re-run against the incumbent before retention.
Admission is a counterfactual A/B test with provenance files; retirement/quarantine and size bounds are not described, and acceptance can be triggered by a same-pool retest.

unassigned: Cross-user aggregation as the headline mechanism has no dedicated domain-card condition.

revision_proposals.text: Consider a condition on aggregation scope (single-user vs pooled sessions) with the matching control, single-source evidence.

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: No original-card counterpart; the domain operation (mine pooled interaction streams into versioned skill packages, gate them, publish) is not a row-for-row instance of any of the 15 original operations.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: Closest RS idea (C03 retrieval conditioning) lacks the write/validate/retain half.

claims.text: Collective skill evolution significantly improves Qwen3-Max on WildClawBench categories.
claims.baseline_control: Day-1 initial skill pool (no concurrent no-evolution control).
claims.selection_vs_test: Validation tasks drawn from daytime tasks of the same benchmark; reported series is the best deployed pool.
claims.result_denominator: Category scores in percent; per-category task counts and run counts not given; single run.
claims.allowed_conclusion: In one small simulated deployment the best-so-far deployed pool scored higher on the same tasks used for validation; the effect size is not separated from run-to-run noise or selection on the benchmark.
Monotonicity of the displayed series follows from carrying forward the best reading; it does not show real improvement or absence of degradation on new tasks.

claims.text: A single evolution round fixes procedural failures (Skill Evolve Lite).
claims.allowed_conclusion: Procedural fixes can be encoded in skills for targeted failures; no generalization claim.

claims.text: Cross-user aggregation enables knowledge transfer and cumulative improvement.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Unsupported by an experiment: no single-user control and no cross-user transfer measure.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A gated skill-evolution loop (agentic evolver, nightly old-vs-new execution, only accepted skills deployed) raised the best-so-far scores of the evolved skill pool on four WildClawBench categories within a 6-round, 8-user simulation; the same-benchmark validation, single run and same-pool retest variation mean the size of the real improvement and the role of cross-user aggregation are unresolved.
not_supported: Generalization to tasks outside the validation pool or to the two unreported categories.
Superiority over other skill-evolution methods (no baselines).
unresolved: History mode (--fresh vs --no-fresh) used in the reported experiment.
assessment.reproduction_note: Author-reported; not reproduced. evidence_level capped at task because selection tasks and reported tasks coincide.

G.reason: Concrete, plausible limitation (static per-user skills, repeated rediscovery) with an identified residue (cross-user aggregation), but the static-library premise is partly contradicted by prior skill-evolution work that the paper cites and does not compare against, so the nearest-neighbor boundary is incomplete.

M.reason: Mechanism is reasoned end-to-end: grouping by skill as a natural controlled factor, joint use of success and failure sessions to protect invariants, separating skill/agent/environment causes, and a counterfactual A/B gate. The cross-user assumption is plausible but the distinguishing prediction against single-user evolution is not tested.

X.reason: The operation chain is highly reconstructable from the main text and appendix prompts: session structuring, grouping, four evolver actions, read-before-write history snapshots with evidence files, nightly A/B, accept/reject, synchronization. Gaps: the validator comparator is model-judged, same-pool retests can be accepted, no retirement/duplicate handling, history persistence depends on an unspecified mode, and cross-user conflicts for environment-specific skills are not addressed.

E.measurement.reason: WildClawBench provides execution-based multi-metric scoring with hard constraints, but the reported daily series is the best deployed pool (a running max) and the accept/reject comparison is delegated to the model; per-category task counts and the metric aggregation used in the plots are not given.

E.causality.reason: Only Day-1 vs later best pool on the same tasks; no no-evolution control run across days, no single-user vs collective control, no evolver ablation, no baseline skill-evolution method. Same-pool retest results indicate readings change without any skill change.

E.holdout.reason: Validation tasks are drawn from the daily interaction data, which are the benchmark tasks being scored; the controlled queries are hand-designed around observed failures; two of six categories are not reported. No held-out tasks or models.

E.statistics.reason: Sample sizes (8 users, 60 tasks, 6 rounds) and many rejected candidates are disclosed, but there is a single run, no variance, intervals or tests, and the reported series is a running best; same-pool retests moved scores by 4.5-8 points without skill change.

E.cost.reason: Authors acknowledge validation adds token cost, but no tokens, dollars, runtime or call counts are given for evolution or validation.
